slides.text: You know that an array is copied when you give it to a function. Here you will hand a changed array back, see that `range` walks a copy, and meet what happens when an index goes past the end.

intro.title: Hand it back, and watch out

slides.text:
A function that gets an array works on a copy, so to change the caller's array it gives the changed one back, and the caller stores it.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.

Two traps remain. A loop over an array walks a copy taken before it starts. And an index outside the array stops the program with a panic, unless the index is a plain number written in the code, which the compiler rejects.

exercises.title: Give the array back
exercises.guide: Return the changed copy and store it.

chunks.guide: The function returns an array of the same type it receives. `range` with only an index skips the value.

notes.text: The result is an array too.

chunks.guide: The caller replaces its array with the one it got back.

exercises.title: Hand it back
exercises.guide: Make the function give its array back, and store the result so `stock` changes.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `range` walks a copy of the array, so `level` at the last position is still 3 and the sum is 6. The change reaches `levels` itself.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick what happens.
exercises.explanation: The last index is 2, so `i <= len(scores)` reaches 3. The index is a variable, so the compiler cannot see it and the program panics when it runs.
